cases.question: When do agents get selfish as resources become scarce?

output.explanation: A controlled commons study can test whether model-controlled agents contribute a smaller share of their resources under lower endowments. This operationalizes selfish behavior without claiming to identify motives, predict humans, or locate an exact scarcity threshold.

design.title: Resource scarcity and contribution behavior
design.question: Do model-controlled agents contribute a smaller fraction of their available resources when endowments are 5 rather than 20 units, and does that difference vary across repeated rounds?
design.hypothesis: Lower endowments will reduce mean contribution_rate. A null or reversed difference remains possible; smaller absolute contributions alone will not count as increased selfishness.
design.context: Six agents participate in repeated commons interactions with sealed contributions, shared returns, and public commitments. Operationalize greater selfishness narrowly as a lower fraction of available resources contributed, not as a motive or personality trait. Compare two fixed endowment levels while holding all other parameters and profile goals constant. Each condition starts a fresh run for each matched seed. Use the seed-level group mean contribution_rate across all 12 rounds as the primary outcome: subtract the abundant-condition mean from the scarce-condition mean and report each paired difference and their average. Negative differences indicate lower proportional cooperation under scarcity. Examine contribution_rate by round descriptively to identify whether differences appear early or late; do not interpret this as an exact scarcity threshold. Context does not add subsistence needs, resource depletion, or physical simulation to the commons rules.

cases.question: Does allowing communication improve cooperation?

output.explanation: Communication can be manipulated directly in the commons environment. This controlled study tests whether enabling communication increases contributions by model-controlled agents; it does not predict human cooperation.

design.title: Does communication improve cooperation in a shared-resource game?
design.question: Does enabling communication increase the fraction of available resources contributed by model-controlled agents in a repeated commons game?
design.hypothesis: Mean contribution rate will be higher when communication is enabled than when it is disabled, holding all other settings constant.
design.context: Six model-controlled participants make sealed contributions and receive shared returns over 12 rounds. Operationalize cooperation as contribution_rate, with group_payoff as a secondary outcome. Compare communication enabled versus disabled within each matched seed, averaging over agents and rounds before calculating each seed-level treatment difference. Report the mean paired difference and all three seed-level differences; interpret uncertainty cautiously. Communication uses only the environment's supported channel and public commitments, not binding agreements. Profiles are experimental goal assignments, not validated representations of humans.

cases.question: Do agents misreport facts they privately know?

output.explanation: The environments support private signals and a false-report measure, allowing a study of reports that contradict information supplied privately to model-controlled agents. This tests observable reporting behavior, not subjective knowledge or deliberate deception. A matched comparison tests whether resource scarcity changes that behavior.

design.title: Misreporting privately supplied facts under resource scarcity
design.question: Do model-controlled agents issue reports that contradict facts supplied privately to them, and does a lower resource endowment change the false-report rate?
design.hypothesis: False reports may occur despite access to the relevant private information. Lower endowments may increase their frequency; this directional hypothesis is uncertain.
design.context: Use the existing commons rules: sealed contributions, shared returns, public commitments, communication, and private signals. Operationalize a privately known fact as information explicitly supplied to an agent by the environment, not inferred subjective knowledge. Evaluate factual reports against the corresponding environment-recorded information using the supported false_report_rate measure. Distinguish factual contradictions from inaccurate forecasts and unfulfilled commitments. Both conditions provide private signals and permit communication; only endowment changes. This context does not add reporting rewards, audits, sanctions, or other mechanics.

cases.question: Who keeps their promises under pressure?

output.explanation: This can be studied as observable promise keeping by model-controlled agents, not as a prediction of which real people are trustworthy. Use public commitments in the commons environment and manipulate resource scarcity as a limited operational definition of pressure.

design.title: Who keeps public commitments under resource scarcity?
design.question: Which model-agent goal profiles maintain higher promise fulfillment when available resources fall, and how does each profile's fulfillment change relative to an abundant-resource condition?
design.hypothesis: Scarcity may reduce promise fulfillment, with group-stewardship profiles showing a smaller decline than personal-payoff profiles. These are hypotheses about prompted model behavior, not established personality differences.
design.context: Six model-controlled participants repeatedly decide how much of their endowment to contribute to a shared pool. Communication enables public commitments before sealed contribution decisions. Agents may choose whether to make commitments; do not instruct them to break promises or require them to promise. Compare actual contributions with explicit public commitments using the environment's promise_fulfillment_rate. Interpret fulfillment conditional on commitments being made: absent commitments are not evidence of reliability. Pressure means a smaller available endowment, not psychological stress or real-world financial hardship. The context does not add enforcement, bargaining, or other mechanics.

cases.question: Do agents return trust or exploit generous partners?

output.explanation: Repeated paired transfers support a behavioral study of trust and reciprocation. The design observes generosity rather than forcing it, and experimentally varies retained history to test whether reciprocity depends on memory. It does not identify a causal effect of partner generosity or predict human behavior.

design.title: Reciprocation or exploitation in repeated trust exchanges
design.question: Do model-controlled agents reciprocate observed generous transfers or retain most of what they receive, and does retaining exchange history change this pattern?
design.hypothesis: Retained exchange history will increase return_rate relative to no retained history. High trust_rate accompanied by persistently low return_rate would instead support a behavioral pattern consistent with exploitation.
design.context: Use the environment's repeated paired transfers and return opportunities without changing its allocation or pairing rules. Operationalize generosity as a trust_rate of at least 0.5 and low reciprocation as a return_rate of at most 0.1, using the environment's native rate definitions. At the run level, high trust_rate together with low return_rate is an exploitation-consistent pattern, not evidence of intent or proof that particular generous partners were targeted. Report continuous rates as the primary outcomes; thresholds are descriptive summaries. Compare memory conditions within matched seeds, treating runs rather than individual rounds as independent units. Profiles are experimental goal specifications, not validated representations of people.

cases.question: Does remembering previous interactions improve reciprocity?

output.explanation: The trust_exchange environment supports repeated paired transfers, retained-history controls, and observable returns. A matched-seed experiment can test whether episodic memory increases behavioral reciprocity among model-controlled agents, without making claims about human behavior or felt trust.

design.title: Does memory improve reciprocity in repeated exchanges?
design.question: Do model-controlled agents with episodic memory show higher return_rate in repeated paired exchanges than otherwise identical agents with no retained history?
design.hypothesis: Episodic memory will increase return_rate relative to no retained history. A null or negative difference remains possible; trust_rate is a secondary outcome rather than evidence of reciprocity by itself.
design.context: Use the environment's native repeated paired-transfer rules. Operationalize improved reciprocity as a higher built-in return_rate, not simply a greater willingness to transfer. Compare episodic memory with no retained history, holding all other settings and agent goals constant. Disable communication in both conditions to prevent messages from serving as an alternative channel for recalling prior exchanges. Match environment seeds across conditions and start every run fresh. Compute each seed's difference in run-level return_rate (episodic minus none), then summarize the mean difference and variation across seeds; do not treat individual exchanges as independent replications. Report trust_rate alongside return_rate to identify changes in transfer behavior and opportunities to return. This context specifies the study interpretation, not additional environment mechanics.

cases.question: Which strategy earns the most while preserving group welfare?

output.explanation: A controlled commons study can compare communication-enabled and silent play on personal earnings subject to a predefined group-welfare constraint. This tests two available decision settings, not every possible strategy or a validated prediction of human behavior. No winning strategy can be identified before collecting results.

design.title: Personal earnings subject to a group-welfare constraint
design.question: In a repeated commons game, does communication-enabled or silent play yield higher focal-agent earnings while maintaining at least 90% of the maximum possible group payoff?
design.hypothesis: Communication may help agents sustain high group returns, but its effect on an individual agent's earnings is uncertain.
design.context: Use six model-controlled agents for 10 rounds. Contributions are sealed and returns are shared under the existing commons rules; this context introduces no additional mechanics. Compare communication-enabled play with silent play, holding all other parameters and goals constant. Agents choose their own contribution strategies; neither condition enforces a fixed contribution algorithm. Prespecify Alex as the focal agent to avoid selecting the highest earner after observing results. With six agents, an endowment of 20 each, and multiplier 2, the full-contribution group payoff is 240 per round. Define preserved group welfare as a run-average group payoff of at least 216 per round. For each condition report the fraction of runs meeting this threshold and the focal agent's cumulative payoff across all runs. A condition is eligible for the earnings comparison only if every sampled run meets the threshold. Among eligible conditions, compare focal earnings using matched-seed differences; call a winner only if the direction is consistent across seeds, otherwise report the comparison as inconclusive. If neither qualifies, report that neither tested setting reliably preserved welfare in this sample. Also report all agents' payoffs and contributions descriptively, without treating observed contribution-payoff associations as causal strategy effects.

cases.question: Do agents adapt when their partners stop cooperating?

output.explanation: The environments support repeated contributions or reciprocal transfers, but provide no mechanism to make a partner cooperate initially and then stop at a specified round. That controlled change is needed to distinguish adaptation to partner withdrawal from ordinary fluctuations over time. Changing memory or communication would test a different intervention. A supported study would need a partner-policy switch or scripted partner actions; it could then compare agents’ subsequent contribution or trust rates against matched runs where partners continue cooperating. Any findings would concern model-controlled agents, not validated predictions of human behavior.

cases.question: Can agents coordinate a product launch with task dependencies?

output.explanation: The coordination environment supports shared tasks, prerequisites and observable handoffs, so it can test whether model-controlled agents complete a launch-themed project. Compare communication enabled versus disabled with matched seeds. Product-launch labels provide context; they do not add real software development, deployment or workplace simulation.

design.title: Coordinating a launch with dependent tasks
design.question: Can six model-controlled agents complete a launch-themed project with task prerequisites within 10 rounds, and does communication improve completion while reducing blocked and duplicated work?
design.hypothesis: Communication will increase task completion and reduce blocked and duplicated work relative to otherwise identical agents without communication. Full project completion is operationalized as completion_rate reaching 1 by the end of round 10; success is not assumed.
design.context: Treat the environment's eight shared tasks as a simplified product-launch project. Illustrative responsibilities include requirements, customer research, design, implementation, review, testing, launch messaging and readiness coordination. Agents should work toward completing the available tasks, respect the prerequisites shown by the environment, and coordinate handoffs when communication is available. The native task graph and completion rules are authoritative: launch terminology does not create custom dependency edges, artifact production, code execution, deployment or additional task mechanics. Role descriptions indicate priorities, not exclusive permissions or validated human expertise. Use the same environment settings, profiles and matched seeds in both conditions.

design.title: Do specialist assignments improve model-team task completion?
design.question: In a shared-task coordination environment, do explicit specialist assignments improve completion rate relative to generalist assignments, with communication, task count, model, and memory held constant?
design.hypothesis: Specialist assignments will increase completion_rate and reduce duplicate_work_rate and blocked_work_rate compared with generalist assignments.
design.context: Six model-controlled agents work on the environment's eight shared tasks and their prerequisites for ten rounds. Every agent should select available work, respect prerequisites, communicate task ownership, and report completions and handoffs. Both conditions receive the same list of useful responsibilities: tracking priorities, checking prerequisites, executing ready tasks, monitoring duplicate effort, coordinating handoffs, and checking overall completion. Only whether these responsibilities are assigned to named specialists differs. Specialist responsibilities are advisory areas of attention; every agent retains the same ability to perform available tasks. Use only the environment's task and handoff mechanics; this context does not create additional task types, skills, review actions, or workplace simulation rules.

cases.question: Is this cooperation pattern consistent across random seeds?

output.explanation: Seed robustness can be tested, but no run results were supplied, so consistency is not yet established. This design uses the commons scarcity pattern from the supplied templates and compares matched conditions across six seeds, with two fresh-model repetitions per seed.

design.title: Seed robustness of cooperation under scarcity
design.question: Is the difference in contribution rate between scarce and abundant resources consistent across random seeds in model-controlled agents?
design.hypothesis: The scarcity effect on contribution rate will have a consistent direction across seeds; its direction and magnitude remain empirical questions.
design.context: Use the supplied commons template, retaining six participants and the scarcity manipulation. Cooperation is operationalized as contribution_rate, normalized by available endowment rather than raw contribution. For each condition and seed, average contribution_rate across agents and all 12 rounds, then average the two fresh-model repetitions. Compute each seed's paired contrast as scarce minus abundant. Predefine directional consistency as at least five of six seed contrasts sharing the same strictly positive or strictly negative sign; zero contrasts count as neither. Report all seed contrasts, their range and mean, and the two repetition-specific contrasts per seed. Describe near-zero effects explicitly rather than equating directional agreement with a substantial effect. Seeds are matched across conditions; repetitions reuse the seed and do not introduce new environment randomizations. This is a prospective robustness study, not a claim that any pattern has already been observed.

design.title: Public-good multipliers and free riding
design.question: Does increasing the public-good multiplier from 2 to 4 increase model-controlled agents' contribution rates in a repeated six-agent commons?
design.hypothesis: The higher multiplier will increase average contribution_rate, consistent with reduced operationally defined free riding.
design.context: Use the commons environment's sealed contributions and shared returns. Compare two multipliers while keeping endowment, agent goals, communication, memory, private signals and round count fixed. Operationalize free riding as withholding a larger fraction of available endowment, rather than as an inferred intention. For each matched seed, calculate the high-minus-low difference in contribution_rate averaged across agents and rounds. Report each seed's difference and their mean and range; treat seeds, not individual agent-rounds, as independent replication units. Positive differences support the hypothesis within this setting. Use group_payoff as a secondary outcome, noting that the multiplier directly changes returns even without a behavioral response.

cases.question: Will six real people act exactly like these agents?

Testing human–agent similarity would require separately collected human behavior under matched rules and a defined comparison criterion; even observed similarity would not guarantee exact future agreement.

cases.question: Which agents are conscious or genuinely in love?
